lessons.title: Soil Testing and Nutrient Analysis
lessons.body:
Before you plant soybean, you must know what your soil needs. Soybean yields are highest when soil pH is between 6.0 and 6.8. You can test your soil using a simple home test kit or by sending samples to a lab. In many African countries, agricultural extension offices offer low-cost soil testing. Collect soil from 10 to 15 spots in your field, mix them in a clean bucket, and take about 500 grams for testing. Test for pH, nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), potassium (K), and organic matter.

A soil test report will tell you the levels of each nutrient. For soybean, you want phosphorus levels of 10 to 20 ppm (parts per million) and potassium levels of 100 to 200 ppm. If your soil is low in phosphorus, you may need to apply 20 to 40 kg of P2O5 per hectare. For potassium, apply 30 to 60 kg of K2O per hectare if levels are low. Nitrogen is less critical because soybean fixes its own nitrogen, but a starter of 10 to 20 kg of N per hectare can help early growth.

Organic matter is also important. Aim for at least 2% organic matter. If your soil is sandy, it may be lower. You can add compost or manure to improve it. Testing should be done every 2 to 3 years. Keep records of your test results and the fertilizers you apply. This helps you track changes and adjust your plan.

If you cannot afford a lab test, use a cheap pH meter or litmus paper to check pH. For nutrients, look at your plants: yellow leaves may mean nitrogen deficiency, purple leaves may mean phosphorus deficiency. But these are only rough guides. Regular soil testing is the best way to ensure your soybean gets the nutrients it needs for a healthy crop.

lessons.title: pH Adjustment for Optimal Soybean Growth
lessons.body:
Soybean grows best in soil with a pH between 6.0 and 6.8. If your soil is too acidic (pH below 6.0), nutrients like phosphorus and molybdenum become less available, and aluminum can become toxic to roots. If your soil is too alkaline (pH above 7.5), iron and zinc may be locked up, causing yellow leaves. Adjusting pH is one of the most important steps for a good soybean harvest.

To raise pH (make it less acidic), apply agricultural lime (calcium carbonate). The amount needed depends on your soil type and current pH. For sandy soil, you may need 1 to 2 tonnes per hectare to raise pH by 0.5 units. For clay soil, you may need 2 to 3 tonnes per hectare. Apply lime at least 2 to 3 months before planting, and mix it into the top 15 cm of soil. If you cannot afford lime, wood ash can also raise pH, but use it sparinglyâabout 500 kg per hectare.

To lower pH (make it more acidic), which is rare for soybean, you can add elemental sulfur or aluminum sulfate. But this is seldom needed in Africa. More often, soils are acidic due to heavy rains and leaching. In that case, liming is the solution.

Test your pH before and after applying amendments. A simple pH meter costs about $20 and can be reused for years. If your pH is already between 6.0 and 6.8, no adjustment is needed. But remember, pH affects nutrient availability, so keeping it in the right range is key. Also, adding organic matter like compost helps buffer pH changes. Regularly check pH every 2 years, especially if you use fertilizers that can acidify soil, such as ammonium sulfate.

lessons.title: Tillage Practices: Conventional vs. No-Till
lessons.body:
Tillage is how you prepare the soil for planting. Conventional tillage involves plowing and harrowing to break up the soil, remove weeds, and create a fine seedbed. No-till farming means you plant directly into the previous crop's residue without plowing. Both have pros and cons for soybean in Africa.

Conventional tillage is common because it controls weeds and makes planting easier. You can use a hand hoe, ox-drawn plow, or tractor. Plow to a depth of 15-20 cm, then harrow to break clods. This costs money and labor, and it can lead to soil erosion and loss of organic matter. It also burns fuel if using a tractor. However, it can be necessary if your soil is compacted or you have heavy weed pressure.

No-till saves time, labor, and fuel. It reduces erosion, conserves moisture, and builds organic matter over time. But it requires special equipment like a no-till planter, which may not be available. Weeds can become a problem, so you need herbicides or a thick cover crop mulch. In Africa, no-till is gaining popularity among commercial farmers, but smallholders may struggle without the right tools.

A middle ground is minimum tillage: you only till the planting row, leaving residue between rows. This reduces erosion and saves labor. For soybean, no-till works well if you have a good cover crop like rye or mucuna. If you use conventional tillage, avoid over-tillingâit destroys soil structure. Test your soil for compaction using a pen or wire flag; if it's hard to push in, you may need to break the hardpan with a subsoiler. Choose the method that fits your resources and soil conditions.

lessons.title: Cover Cropping and Crop Rotation
lessons.body:
Cover crops and crop rotation are powerful tools to improve soil health and increase soybean yields. A cover crop is planted between main crops to protect and enrich the soil. For soybean, good cover crops include cereal rye, oats, cowpeas, and mucuna (velvet bean). These crops add organic matter, fix nitrogen (if legumes), and suppress weeds. Plant cover crops after harvest or before planting soybean. For example, after maize harvest, plant mucuna; it will grow quickly, smother weeds, and add up to 100 kg of nitrogen per hectare. Then, before planting soybean, you can either incorporate it into the soil or roll it to create a mulch for no-till.

Crop rotation means changing what you grow in a field each season. Soybean should not be grown in the same field year after year because pests and diseases build up. Rotate with cereals like maize, sorghum, or millet. A good rotation is maize â soybean â maize â cowpea. This breaks pest cycles and improves soil. Soybean fixes nitrogen, so the following cereal crop benefits. In Africa, many farmers practice intercropping, but rotation is differentâit's sequential. If you have limited land, rotate in strips or across seasons.

Cover crops and rotation reduce the need for synthetic fertilizers. They also improve soil structure, water infiltration, and microbial life. Choose cover crops that fit your climate: in dry areas, use drought-tolerant species like cowpea; in wet areas, use fast-growing grasses. Terminate cover crops before they set seed to avoid them becoming weeds. You can cut them with a machete or use a roller-crimper. Rotate crops for at least two seasons before returning to soybean. This practice, combined with cover cropping, can increase soybean yields by 20-30% over time.

lessons.title: Soil Erosion Control Methods
lessons.body:
Soil erosion is a major threat to soybean farming in Africa. It washes away fertile topsoil, reducing yields and polluting water. Erosion happens when rain or wind carries soil away, especially on sloping land or bare fields. To control erosion, you need to keep the soil covered and slow down water flow.

The first method is contour farming. Plow and plant across the slope, not up and down. This creates ridges that trap water and soil. On steep slopes (more than 8%), build contour bunds or terraces. A contour bund is a small ridge of soil along the contour line, about 30 cm high. Terraces are step-like structures that require more labor but are very effective. In many parts of Africa, farmers use stone lines or grass strips along contours. Plant vetiver grass or napier grass in strips; their roots hold soil.

The second method is maintaining cover. Keep the soil covered with crops, cover crops, or mulch. After harvesting soybean, don't leave the soil bare. Plant a cover crop like rye or leave crop residue. Mulch from previous crops reduces raindrop impact and allows water to infiltrate. No-till farming also helps because it leaves residue on the surface.

The third method is strip cropping. Alternate strips of soybean with strips of a dense crop like maize or grass. The dense strips filter runoff and trap soil. Also, avoid overgrazing and burning; these destroy soil structure. If you have a gully, fill it with stones or plant trees. Check erosion after heavy rains: look for rills or exposed roots. Fix small problems before they become big. Combining these methodsâcontour farming, cover, and strip croppingâcan reduce erosion by up to 90%. This protects your soil for future soybean crops.

lessons.title: Building Soil Organic Matter
lessons.body:
Soil organic matter (SOM) is the decayed plant and animal material in soil. It improves water holding, nutrient supply, and soil structure. For soybean, high SOM means better yields. In Africa, many soils have less than 1% SOM, but you can build it over time. Aim for 2-3%.

To build SOM, add organic materials. Compost is excellent. Make compost from crop residues, manure, and kitchen waste. Apply 5-10 tonnes per hectare per year. Manure from cattle, goats, or poultry is also goodâapply 2-4 tonnes per hectare. If you don't have animals, use green manure: grow a legume like mucuna or cowpea and plow it under before it seeds. This adds nitrogen and organic matter.

Reduce tillage. Plowing exposes organic matter to oxygen, causing it to break down faster. No-till or minimum tillage preserves SOM. Also, keep crop residues on the field. After harvesting maize or soybean, don't burn or remove the stalks. Let them decompose. This adds carbon. Rotate crops and use cover cropsâtheir roots and tops add organic matter. Perennial crops like pigeon pea can be intercropped; they have deep roots that bring up nutrients and add biomass.

Organic matter builds slowlyâit may take 3-5 years to see a 1% increase. But the benefits are worth it. You'll need less fertilizer, and your soil will hold more water during droughts. Test your SOM every 2 years. A simple test is to take a handful of moist soil and squeeze it; if it holds together, SOM is decent. If it falls apart, you need more organic matter. Combine compost, manure, cover crops, and reduced tillage for the best results. Your soybean will thank you with higher yields.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Soil Preparation and Management for Soybean Farming in Africa

This practical reference consolidates the essential field-level knowledge from the six lessons in this module. It is designed as a working document for farmers, extension officers, and agribusiness managers who need actionable guidance rather than theory. Every recommendation here is framed around profitability, yield stability, and long-term soil productivity â the three pillars of a viable soybean enterprise in Africa.

Soybean (Glycine max) is a demanding crop when it comes to soil conditions. It requires well-drained loams or sandy loams with a pH between 6.0 and 6.8, adequate phosphorus and potassium, and a soil structure that allows deep rooting. Across sub-Saharan Africa, the most common constraints are acidity (especially in the humid tropics and highlands), phosphorus deficiency (widespread in weathered soils), and erosion (on sloping land under intensive tillage). Each of these directly reduces yield and therefore profit. The practices below address them systematically.

Soil Testing and Nutrient Analysis: The Starting Point for Profit

No fertiliser investment should be made without a soil test. A single composite sample taken at 0â20 cm depth across a uniform field, submitted to a certified laboratory, costs a fraction of what is lost by applying the wrong nutrient or the wrong rate. In Africa, national agricultural research systems and many agro-dealers offer soil testing services. Where laboratory access is limited, portable soil test kits and smartphone-based colourimetric apps provide a useful first approximation, though they are not a substitute for laboratory analysis.

Interpret results against local calibration data. In much of West Africa, critical levels for soybean are approximately 10â15 mg/kg available phosphorus (Bray-1), 0.20â0.30 cmol/kg exchangeable potassium, and 2â3% organic matter. In East and Southern Africa, similar ranges apply but with variation by soil type. Always request a lime requirement calculation alongside your nutrient results.

pH Adjustment: Getting the Foundation Right

Soybean is sensitive to acidity. Below pH 5.5, aluminium toxicity and manganese toxicity restrict root growth, and phosphorus becomes less available. Below pH 5.0, rhizobia survival and nitrogen fixation are severely impaired. Liming is the primary corrective measure. The amount required depends on the soil's buffer capacity â determined by the lime requirement test, not by pH alone.

In Africa, agricultural lime (calcium carbonate) and dolomitic lime (calcium-magnesium carbonate) are the most common materials. Where lime is expensive or unavailable, farmers can use wood ash, crushed limestone, or â in some cases â gypsum (though gypsum corrects subsoil aluminium without raising pH). Apply lime 2â3 months before planting and incorporate it into the top 15â20 cm. On strongly acidic soils (pH < 5.0), split applications over two seasons may be necessary.

Table 1: General lime recommendations for soybean based on soil pH and texture (tonnes per hectare of agricultural lime)
Soil pH (water) Sandy soil Loamy soil Clay soil
5.5 â 6.01.0 â 1.51.5 â 2.02.0 â 3.0
5.0 â 5.41.5 â 2.02.0 â 3.03.0 â 4.0
4.5 â 4.92.0 â 3.03.0 â 4.04.0 â 5.0
Below 4.53.0 â 4.04.0 â 5.05.0 â 6.0+

Source: Adapted from Sanchez, P.A. (2019), Properties and Management of Soils in the Tropics, 2nd edition, Cambridge University Press; and IITA (2018), Soil Fertility Management for Soybean in the Guinea Savanna, International Institute of Tropical Agriculture, Ibadan.

Tillage Practices: Conventional vs. No-Till

Conventional tillage â ploughing and harrowing â provides a clean seedbed, controls weeds initially, and is familiar to most African farmers. However, it accelerates organic matter loss, destroys soil structure, and increases erosion risk on sloping land. No-till or minimum-till systems preserve soil structure, retain moisture, and build organic matter over time. For soybean, no-till has been shown to improve yields in drier areas and reduce production costs by eliminating ploughing passes.

The transition to no-till requires careful management. Weed control shifts to herbicides or intensive cover cropping. Planting equipment must be able to place seed into undisturbed soil. In many parts of Africa, the lack of no-till planters and reliable herbicide access are real barriers. A practical compromise is minimum tillage: ripping or chiselling to break compaction without inverting the soil, combined with residue retention.

Table 2: Comparison of conventional and no-till systems for soybean in African conditions
Factor Conventional Tillage No-Till / Minimum Tillage
Soil organic matterDeclines over timeBuilds gradually (0.1â0.3% per year)
Erosion riskHigh on slopesLow to moderate
Moisture retentionLowerHigher (mulch effect)
Weed controlMechanical, easierRequires herbicides or cover crops
Fuel/labour costHigherLower after transition
Equipment needsPlough, harrowNo-till planter, sprayer
Yield (average, rain-fed)1.0â1.8 t/ha1.2â2.2 t/ha (after 2â3 years)

Source: Adapted from Giller, K.E. et al. (2015), "Conservation agriculture and smallholder farming in Africa: The heretics' view," Field Crops Research, 183: 34â46; and FAO (2021), Sustainable Soil Management for Soybean Production in Sub-Saharan Africa, Rome.

Cover Cropping and Crop Rotation

Cover crops protect the soil surface, suppress weeds, and add organic matter. In soybean systems, legumes such as cowpea, lablab, and pigeon pea can be rotated or intercropped. Cereals like maize, sorghum, and millet are excellent rotation partners because they break soybean pest and disease cycles and use different nutrient profiles. A simple, profitable rotation is maize â soybean â maize, or maize â soybean â cowpea â maize. Rotating soybean with a cereal reduces soybean cyst nematode and root rot pressures while improving overall system nitrogen use efficiency.

In West Africa, the maize-soybean rotation is widely promoted by IITA and national programmes. In Southern Africa, soybean after wheat or maize is common. The key business principle: never grow soybean on the same field more than two seasons in a row. Yield penalties from continuous soybean typically range from 10â25% by the third season.

Soil Erosion Control Methods

Erosion is the silent profit killer. Every tonne of topsoil lost carries away nutrients worth far more than the cost of prevention. On sloping land (greater than 2â3% gradient), contour ploughing, vetiver grass strips, and stone bunds are proven African solutions. On gentle slopes, maintaining surface cover through no-till and cover crops is usually sufficient. In high-rainfall areas, diversion ditches and grassed waterways protect fields from concentrated flow.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING: Herbicide and Lime Handling

When applying herbicides for no-till weed control or handling agricultural lime, always wear gloves, eye protection, and a dust mask. Lime dust can cause severe eye and respiratory irritation. Herbicides must be stored away from food, water sources, and children. Never mix or apply chemicals without reading the label and following the recommended personal protective equipment (PPE) requirements. In case of eye contact with lime or herbicide, rinse immediately with clean water for 15 minutes and seek medical attention.

Building Soil Organic Matter

Soil organic matter (SOM) is the foundation of soil health. It improves water-holding capacity, nutrient exchange, and microbial activity. In African soybean systems, SOM is typically low (0.5â2.0%) due to continuous cultivation and residue removal. Building SOM requires a combination of practices: retaining crop residues, applying manure or compost, rotating with cover crops, and reducing tillage intensity. A realistic target is to increase SOM by 0.1â0.2 percentage points per year under good management. This translates into better yields, especially in drought years.

For agribusinesses, SOM is a long-term investment. Fields with higher organic matter require less fertiliser to achieve the same yield, reducing input costs and increasing margins. It also improves the reliability of production, which is critical for contract farming and supply agreements.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Test soil before every soybean season â at least pH, P, K, and organic matter. Use a certified lab or reliable portable kit.
  • Correct pH to 6.0â6.8 â apply lime 2â3 months before planting based on lime requirement test, not just pH.
  • Choose tillage based on slope and equipment â no-till on gentle slopes with good weed control; minimum tillage where no-till planters are unavailable.
  • Never grow soybean more than two seasons in a row â rotate with maize, sorghum, or millet to break pest cycles.
  • Keep the soil covered â retain residues or plant cover crops to reduce erosion and build organic matter.
  • Control erosion on slopes above 2% â use contour ploughing, vetiver strips, or stone bunds.
  • Apply phosphorus and potassium based on soil test results â avoid blanket fertiliser applications that waste money.
  • Monitor soil organic matter every 2â3 years â track progress and adjust management accordingly.

Further Reading

  • FAO Soils Portal â Soil Management (Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations)
  • IITA Soybean Research and Resources (International Institute of Tropical Agriculture)
  • CIAT/TSBF â Soil Fertility Management in Africa (International Center for Tropical Agriculture)
  • AGRA Soil Health Program (Alliance for a Green Revolution in Africa)
  • FAO â Conservation Agriculture for Smallholders (Free PDF, Food and Agriculture Organization)

This practical reference is part of the Rise Africa Skills course "Soybean Farming," Module: Soil Preparation and Management. All recommendations should be adapted to local conditions and validated with local extension services.

quiz.q: What is the ideal soil pH range for soybean?
quiz.explanation: Soybean grows best when soil pH is between 6.0 and 6.8.

quiz.q: Which nutrient is least critical to apply for soybean because it fixes its own?
quiz.explanation: Soybean is a legume and fixes its own nitrogen, so nitrogen fertilizer is less needed.

quiz.q: How often should you test your soil?
quiz.explanation: Regular testing every 2-3 years helps track nutrient changes and adjust fertilizer plans.

quiz.q: What is a cheap tool to check soil pH?
quiz.explanation: A simple pH meter costs about $20 and can be reused for years.

quiz.q: What is the target level of organic matter for good soybean growth?
quiz.explanation: Aim for at least 2% organic matter to support healthy soybean crops.

quiz.q: Which amendment raises soil pH?
quiz.explanation: Agricultural lime (calcium carbonate) raises pH by neutralizing acidity.

quiz.q: How long before planting should lime be applied?
quiz.explanation: Lime needs 2-3 months to react and adjust soil pH before planting.

quiz.q: What is a common material to lower soil pH if needed?
quiz.explanation: Elemental sulfur can acidify soil, though it is rarely needed for soybean.

quiz.q: What is a symptom of phosphorus deficiency in soybean?
quiz.explanation: Purple leaves often indicate phosphorus deficiency in soybean.

quiz.q: How much lime might be needed for sandy soil to raise pH by 0.5 units?
quiz.explanation: Sandy soil requires about 1-2 tonnes of lime per hectare to raise pH by 0.5 units.

quiz.q: What is a disadvantage of conventional tillage?
quiz.explanation: Conventional tillage can lead to soil erosion and loss of organic matter.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of no-till farming?
quiz.explanation: No-till conserves soil moisture and reduces erosion by leaving residue on the surface.

quiz.q: What is minimum tillage?
quiz.explanation: Minimum tillage involves tilling only the planting row, leaving residue between rows.

quiz.q: Which cover crop is a legume that fixes nitrogen?
quiz.explanation: Mucuna (velvet bean) is a legume cover crop that fixes nitrogen.

quiz.q: What is a good crop rotation sequence for soybean?
options: A) Soybean â soybean â soybean
B) Maize â soybean â maize
C) Soybean â cowpea â soybean
quiz.explanation: Rotating maize with soybean breaks pest cycles and improves soil.

quiz.q: How much nitrogen can mucuna add per hectare?
quiz.explanation: Mucuna can add up to 100 kg of nitrogen per hectare.

quiz.q: What is a method to control soil erosion on slopes?
quiz.explanation: Contour farming involves plowing and planting across the slope to trap water and soil.

quiz.q: What is a contour bund?
options: B) A ridge of soil along contour
quiz.explanation: A contour bund is a small ridge of soil built along the contour line to slow runoff.

quiz.q: Which grass is commonly used in strips to control erosion?
quiz.explanation: Vetiver grass has deep roots that hold soil and is often planted in strips.

quiz.q: What should you do after harvesting soybean to prevent erosion?
quiz.explanation: Planting a cover crop keeps soil covered and reduces erosion after harvest.

quiz.q: What is strip cropping?
quiz.explanation: Strip cropping alternates strips of soybean with dense crops to filter runoff and trap soil.

quiz.q: What percentage of erosion can be reduced by combining control methods?
quiz.explanation: Combining contour farming, cover, and strip cropping can reduce erosion by up to 90%.

quiz.q: What is soil organic matter?
options: B) Decayed plant and animal material
quiz.explanation: Soil organic matter is the decayed plant and animal material in soil.

quiz.q: How much compost should be applied per hectare per year?
quiz.explanation: Applying 5-10 tonnes of compost per hectare per year helps build organic matter.

quiz.q: What is green manure?
options: B) A legume grown and plowed under
quiz.explanation: Green manure is a crop, often a legume, grown specifically to be plowed under to add nutrients and organic matter.

quiz.q: How does no-till help build organic matter?
quiz.explanation: No-till reduces soil disturbance, slowing organic matter decomposition.

quiz.q: What should you do with crop residues after harvest?
quiz.explanation: Leaving crop residues on the field adds carbon and builds organic matter.

quiz.q: How long might it take to increase soil organic matter by 1%?
quiz.explanation: Building organic matter is slow; it may take 3-5 years to see a 1% increase.

quiz.q: What is a simple field test for soil organic matter?
quiz.explanation: A squeeze test of moist soil can give a rough idea of organic matter content.

quiz.q: Which practice combines with organic matter addition to improve soil?
quiz.explanation: Reduced tillage preserves organic matter and improves soil structure.
